unit: Ch 3: Risk Assessment and Internal Control
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Audit Risk & Its Components
explain: Audit risk is the possibility that the auditor expresses an inappropriate opinion when financial statements are materially misstated.
It happens when an unmodified report is issued on financial statements containing uncorrected material errors or fraud.
Audit risk is a combination of Risks of Material Misstatement (RMM) and Detection Risk.
It excludes the auditor's commercial risks such as loss from litigation, adverse publicity, or poor engagement profitability.

flow.title: How Audit Risk Arises and Is Managed
steps: Auditor procedures fail to catch errors
Auditor lowers Detection Risk to control overall Audit Risk

topics.example: A company inflates year-end sales by Rs 20 Crore using fake invoices, and the auditor fails to detect it and issues a clean report.
remember: Audit Risk = Risk of Material Misstatement × Detection Risk.
mistakes: Including business risks of the auditor (like legal suits or bad publicity) under the technical definition of Audit Risk.

quiz.q: Which of the following is included in technical Audit Risk under SA 200?
o: Risk of loss from client litigation
Risk of expressing an unmodified opinion on materially misstated financial statements
Risk of adverse publicity for the audit firm
Risk of loss of future audit clients
quiz.why: Audit risk strictly refers to expressing an inappropriate opinion on materially misstated financial statements.

quiz.q: Audit Risk is a mathematical function of which two elements?
o: Risk of Material Misstatement and Detection Risk
quiz.why: Audit Risk = Risks of Material Misstatement (RMM) × Detection Risk.

topics.title: Risks of Material Misstatement (RMM) - FS Level & Assertion Level
explain: RMM is the probability that financial statements are materially misstated prior to the audit.
Overall Financial Statement Level risks are pervasive and affect the financial statements as a whole (e.g., weak management governance).
Assertion Level risks relate to specific classes of transactions, account balances, and disclosures (e.g., valuation of obsolete inventory).
Assertion level RMM consists of two entity-owned components: Inherent Risk and Control Risk.

flow.title: Hierarchy of Risks of Material Misstatement
steps: Classify: Overall FS Level vs Assertion Level
Break Assertion Level into Inherent & Control Risk
Design Audit Responses based on Level

topics.example: Rapid technological change causing electronic inventory obsolescence is an assertion-level risk affecting inventory valuation.
remember: Inherent risk and control risk belong to the entity and cannot be directly changed by the auditor.
mistakes: Assuming overall financial statement level risks are restricted to a single account balance.

quiz.q: Risks that affect the financial statements as a whole and potentially influence many assertions are termed as:
o: Pervasive / Overall financial statement level risks
quiz.why: Overall financial statement level risks are pervasive in nature and affect the entire financial reporting process.

quiz.q: Which of the following components of RMM exists independently of the audit of financial statements?
quiz.why: Both Inherent Risk and Control Risk are entity risks that exist independently of the financial statement audit.

topics.title: Inherent Risk & Control Risk
explain: Inherent Risk is the susceptibility of an assertion to material misstatement before considering any related internal controls.
It depends on the nature of business, complexity of calculations, judgment involved, and asset vulnerability to theft.
Control Risk is the risk that internal controls will fail to prevent, or detect and correct, a material misstatement on a timely basis.
Control Risk has an inverse relationship with internal control efficiency: higher control efficiency means lower control risk.

flow.title: Difference and Relationship between Inherent & Control Risk
steps: Inherent Risk present due to nature/complexity
Control Risk present if controls fail/are bypassed

topics.example: Cash is inherently risky due to easy theft (Inherent Risk); leaving cash safes unlocked creates high Control Risk.
remember: High internal control efficiency = Low control risk.
mistakes: Confusing Control Risk with Inherent Risk; Inherent Risk ignores internal controls completely.

quiz.q: The susceptibility of an assertion to misstatement before considering any related internal controls is:
quiz.why: Inherent risk is assessed before taking any related internal controls into consideration.

quiz.q: If an entity has very efficient and strong internal controls, its Control Risk will be:
quiz.why: Control risk and internal control efficiency share an inverse relationship; strong controls result in low control risk.

topics.title: Detection Risk & Combined Risk Assessment
explain: Detection Risk is the risk that auditor procedures will fail to detect an existing material misstatement.
It consists of Sampling Risk (sample not representative) and Non-Sampling Risk (human error/inappropriate procedure).
The auditor can directly control and reduce detection risk by expanding testing scope, larger samples, and experienced staff.
There is an inverse relationship between RMM and Detection Risk: higher assessed RMM requires lower target Detection Risk.

flow.title: Combined Risk Assessment Process
steps: Assess Inherent Risk and Control Risk (RMM)
Adjust Nature, Timing, Extent of Substantive Tests
Execute Audit Procedures to lower Detection Risk

topics.example: If an auditor skips attending year-end inventory counting for a large warehouse, non-sampling detection risk increases.
remember: Auditor can only influence Detection Risk; RMM belongs to the client.
mistakes: Thinking that an auditor can reduce Inherent Risk or Control Risk directly.

quiz.q: Which component of Audit Risk is directly controllable by the auditor?
quiz.why: The auditor can directly reduce detection risk by modifying the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures.

quiz.q: When assessed Risk of Material Misstatement (RMM) is HIGH, acceptable Detection Risk must be set at:
quiz.why: RMM and Detection Risk have an inverse relationship. High RMM requires low Detection Risk to keep Audit Risk low.

topics.title: Identifying and Assessing RMM & Risk Assessment Procedures
explain: Risk Assessment Procedures (RAP) are performed to obtain an understanding of the entity, its environment, and internal control.
RAP includes: (a) Inquiries of management and internal staff, (b) Analytical procedures, and (c) Observation and inspection.
RAP provides a basis for identifying and assessing RMM at financial statement and assertion levels.
RAP alone does not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an audit opinion; further testing is needed.

flow.title: Flow of Risk Assessment Procedures
steps: Identify and assess RMM at FS & Assertion levels

topics.example: Performing a walkthrough of the sales cycle by tracing an order from initiation to general ledger posting.
remember: Inquiry alone is not sufficient to obtain audit evidence on control implementation or effectiveness.
mistakes: Issuing an audit report based solely on Risk Assessment Procedures without performing substantive audit testing.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard Risk Assessment Procedure under SA 315?
quiz.why: Issuing an opinion is the final audit outcome, not a risk assessment procedure.

quiz.q: What is a 'walkthrough test' in auditing?
o: Tracing a few transactions from initiation to final reporting
quiz.why: A walkthrough involves tracing a transaction through the information system to understand processing and controls.

topics.title: Concept of Materiality & Auditor's Responsibility
explain: Misstatements, including omissions, are material if they could reasonably influence the economic decisions of users.
Materiality is applied in planning, performing audit procedures, and evaluating the effect of misstatements.
Materiality is not always based on size; small amounts can be material due to their qualitative nature or statutory requirements.
The auditor exercises professional judgment when determining materiality levels and choosing appropriate benchmarks.

flow.title: Applying Materiality in an Audit
steps: Determine Overall Materiality for Financial Statements

topics.example: Division I Schedule III requires separate disclosure of any expense item exceeding 1% of revenue or Rs 1,00,000, making it material by law.
remember: Statutory disclosure requirements make items material regardless of value.
mistakes: Viewing materiality strictly as a quantitative percentage while ignoring qualitative factors.

quiz.q: Under SA 320, misstatements are considered material if they:
o: Could reasonably influence economic decisions of users
quiz.why: Materiality definition focuses on influencing the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of financial statements.

quiz.q: Which standard on auditing deals with Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit?
quiz.why: SA 320 specifically deals with materiality in planning and performing an audit.

topics.title: Use of Benchmarks & Performance Materiality
explain: Benchmarking involves applying a percentage to a chosen financial figure (e.g., Profit Before Tax, Revenue, Net Assets) to set overall materiality.
Profit before tax from continuing operations is commonly used for profit-oriented commercial entities.
Performance Materiality is set at a lower amount than overall materiality to reduce the risk of aggregate undetected errors exceeding overall materiality.
Materiality must be documented, including overall materiality, performance materiality, and any revisions made during audit.

flow.title: Benchmark to Performance Materiality Calculation
steps: Select Benchmark (e.g., Profit Before Tax = Rs 50 Cr)
Apply Percentage (e.g., 4% = Rs 2 Cr Overall Materiality)
Set Performance Materiality lower (e.g., Rs 75 Lakhs)
Perform Audit Procedures using Performance Materiality limit

topics.example: If overall materiality is Rs 2 Crore, performance materiality may be set at Rs 75 Lakhs so individual smaller misstatements don't sum up past Rs 2 Crore.
mistakes: Using volatile single-year low profit as a benchmark without adjusting/normalizing past trends.

quiz.q: Why does an auditor establish 'Performance Materiality' lower than overall materiality?
o: To reduce the probability that aggregate uncorrected misstatements exceed overall materiality
quiz.why: Performance materiality acts as a buffer to catch small misstatements before they aggregate to exceed overall materiality.

quiz.q: Which benchmark is generally chosen for profit-oriented entities operating under normal conditions?
o: Profit Before Tax from continuing operations
quiz.why: Profit before tax from continuing operations is the primary focus for users of profit-oriented entities.

topics.title: Understanding the Entity and Its Environment
explain: Obtaining an understanding of the entity and its environment is a continuous, dynamic process maintained throughout the audit.
It includes: (a) Industry, regulatory, external factors, (b) Nature of entity & operations, (c) Accounting policies, (d) Objectives & strategies, and (e) Performance measurement.
Understanding business risks helps identify potential financial statement misstatements.
Without adequate knowledge of the client's business, a proper and effective audit cannot be planned or executed.
topics.example: An auditor studying a telecom firm checks regulatory changes, licensing fees, and user growth trends.
remember: Understanding the entity is a continuous process, not a one-time setup activity.
mistakes: Assuming that auditing similar companies in the past eliminates the need to understand the current client's specific business.

quiz.q: Obtaining an understanding of the entity and its environment is considered a:
o: One-time activity done on first day of audit
Continuous, dynamic process throughout the audit
Procedure done only after issuing audit report
Task restricted to statutory audits of listed firms
quiz.why: SA 315 defines understanding the entity as a continuous, dynamic process of gathering and updating information.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of understanding the entity under SA 315?
o: Nature of entity and its operations
Personal financial wealth of minority shareholders
Measurement and review of financial performance
quiz.why: Personal wealth of minority shareholders is irrelevant to understanding the entity's business operations and audit risks.

topics.title: Internal Control - Definition, Purpose & Inherent Limitations
explain: Internal control is the process designed, implemented, and maintained by TCWG and management to provide reasonable assurance.
Objectives: Reliable financial reporting, operational efficiency, asset safeguarding, and statutory compliance.
Internal controls can provide only reasonable (not absolute) assurance due to inherent limitations.
Limitations include: human judgment errors, lack of understanding, collusion between staff, management override, and cost-benefit trade-offs.

flow.title: Internal Control Framework & Constraints
steps: Management designs controls for entity objectives

topics.example: Two finance officers conspire to override automated purchase order checks, circumventing segregation of duties.
remember: Internal controls provide reasonable assurance, never absolute assurance.
mistakes: Expecting internal control systems to completely eliminate fraud risks in an organization.

quiz.q: Internal control can provide management and auditors with only:
quiz.why: Inherent limitations of internal control prevent it from providing absolute assurance.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an inherent limitation of internal control?
o: Collusion among employees to bypass controls
quiz.why: Collusion among two or more individuals allows controls to be circumvented.

topics.title: Five Components of Internal Control
explain: 1. Control Environment: Tone at the top, governance, ethics, organizational structure, HR policies.
2. Entity's Risk Assessment Process: How management identifies, estimates, and manages business risks.
3. Information System & Communication: System for recording, processing, and reporting transactions.
4. Control Activities: Policies and procedures like approvals, reconciliations, physical security, segregation of duties.
5. Monitoring of Controls: Management's ongoing or separate evaluation of control performance over time.
topics.example: Ensuring the officer recording a cash payment cannot approve the voucher is a Control Activity (Segregation of Duties).
remember: 5 Components: Control Environment, Risk Assessment, Info System, Control Activities, Monitoring.
mistakes: Treating Control Environment as sufficient on its own without specific Control Activities.

quiz.q: Which component of internal control sets the overall ethical tone and control consciousness of an organization?
quiz.why: Control environment includes governance, ethical values, and management philosophy that set the organizational tone.

quiz.q: Segregation of duties and physical security of assets fall under which component of internal control?
quiz.why: Control Activities are specific policies and procedures like segregation of duties and physical safeguards.

topics.title: Relevant Controls & Understanding Design & Implementation
explain: Not all controls in an entity are relevant to an audit; auditor focuses primarily on controls relevant to financial reporting.
Auditor evaluates control design first to see if it can prevent/detect misstatements.
An improperly designed control represents a significant deficiency.
Implementation means the control exists and the entity is actively using it (verified via walkthroughs, inspection, inquiry, observation).

flow.title: Evaluating Controls: Design vs Implementation
steps: If design is proper, verify Implementation
Determine whether to test operating effectiveness

topics.example: Password controls over ledger access are relevant to audit; automated systems maintaining flight schedules in an airline are generally not.
remember: Evaluate Design FIRST; do not test implementation of an improperly designed control.
mistakes: Assuming inquiry alone is sufficient to test control implementation.

quiz.q: When evaluating internal controls, what must the auditor evaluate FIRST?
o: Operating effectiveness over the full year
quiz.why: There is no point testing implementation or operating effectiveness if the control is designed improperly.

quiz.q: Can inquiry alone provide sufficient audit evidence regarding implementation of a control?
o: Yes, if made to senior directors
No, inquiry must be combined with inspection or observation
quiz.why: Inquiry alone is not sufficient to evaluate design and implementation of controls.

topics.title: Significant Risks (Risks Requiring Special Audit Consideration)
explain: Significant risks are identified inherent risks that require special audit consideration.
Factors evaluated: (a) Fraud risk, (b) Recent economic/regulatory developments, (c) Transaction complexity, (d) Related party transactions, (e) Subjectivity in estimates.
Fraud risks and non-routine related-party transactions outside normal business course are ALWAYS significant risks.
Significant non-routine transactions carry greater RMM due to management intervention, manual processing, and complex accounting.

flow.title: Identifying Significant Risks
steps: Identify non-routine, complex, or fraud-prone areas
Evaluate likelihood and magnitude of potential error
Classify items meeting criteria as 'Significant Risk'
Design specific responsive substantive audit procedures

topics.example: Determining fair values for complex unquoted financial derivatives or significant out-of-course related party asset transfers.
remember: Fraud risks are ALWAYS significant risks under SA 315.
mistakes: Classifying routine, automated, high-volume transactions as significant risks.

quiz.q: Which of the following is ALWAYS considered a significant risk requiring special audit consideration?
o: Risk of material misstatement due to fraud
quiz.why: Risks of material misstatement due to fraud are explicitly classified as always being significant risks.

quiz.q: Why are significant non-routine transactions prone to higher risk of material misstatement?
o: They occur every day with standard software
They involve greater management intervention and manual processing
They have zero impact on tax liabilities
They are audited by internal auditors daily
quiz.why: Non-routine items involve manual intervention, complex calculations, and custom accounting decisions.

topics.title: Methods of Evaluating Internal Control Systems
explain: Auditors use four standard methods to record and evaluate internal control systems:
1. Narrative Record: Complete written description of the system; best for small entities without formal controls.
2. Check List: Series of instructions/questions completed by audit staff with Yes/No/NA ticks.
3. Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ): Comprehensive series of questions answered by client management/staff.
4. Flow Chart: Graphic presentation showing end-to-end transaction flow and documentation.

flow.title: Selecting Evaluation Tool by Entity Type
steps: Use Narrative Record for small/informal entity
Use ICQ / Checklist for medium enterprises
Draw Flowchart for complex multi-department workflows

topics.example: An auditor draws a flowchart mapping sales order receipt, credit approval, warehouse dispatch, billing, and ledger entry.
remember: ICQ: 'Yes' usually means satisfactory position; 'No' indicates potential control weakness.
mistakes: Using narrative records for large complex companies where tracking changes in prose becomes difficult.

quiz.q: Which method of evaluating internal control provides a concise graphical presentation of transaction flows?
quiz.why: A flowchart is a graphic presentation of each part of the internal control system.

quiz.q: In a standard Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ), a 'NO' response generally indicates:
quiz.why: In ICQs, 'Yes' indicates satisfactory position, while 'No' highlights a control gap or weakness.

topics.title: Testing of Internal Controls (Test of Controls)
explain: Test of Controls (ToC) is performed to obtain evidence about the operating effectiveness of controls in preventing/detecting errors throughout the period.
ToC is required when: (a) Auditor plans to rely on control effectiveness to reduce substantive testing, or (b) Substantive procedures alone are insufficient.
Testing methods: Inquiry combined with inspection, observation, re-performance, and testing IT application controls.
Absence of misstatements in substantive tests does NOT automatically prove controls are operating effectively.

flow.title: Testing Operating Effectiveness of Controls
steps: Assess initial reliance on internal controls
Re-evaluate control risk and substantive test scope

topics.example: Re-performing bank reconciliations for selected months to confirm whether supervisory reviews took place consistently.
remember: Inquiry alone is NOT sufficient to test operating effectiveness of controls.
mistakes: Assuming zero detected substantive errors means internal controls operated perfectly all year.

quiz.q: Test of controls is performed to obtain audit evidence regarding:
o: The exact mathematical balance of general ledger
Operating effectiveness of internal controls throughout the period
quiz.why: Tests of controls test whether controls operated effectively at relevant times during the audit period.

quiz.q: If deviations from prescribed controls are detected during testing, the auditor should:
o: Make specific inquiries and determine if substantive tests need expansion
Issue a disclaimer of opinion without further work
quiz.why: Deviations require inquiries to understand reasons and potential reassessment of control risk and substantive testing scope.

topics.title: Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks & Substantive Procedures
explain: Auditor designs overall responses for FS-level risks (e.g., senior staff assignment, professional skepticism, unpredictable tests).
For assertion-level risks, auditor designs further procedures matching assessed risk: ToC and Substantive Procedures.
Substantive procedures comprise: (i) Tests of Details (vouching transactions & verifying balances), and (ii) Substantive Analytical Procedures.
Irrespective of assessed RMM, auditor MUST perform substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, balance, and disclosure.

flow.title: Audit Procedure Structure under SA 330
steps: Determine mix of ToC and Substantive Procedures
Evaluate overall sufficiency of audit evidence

topics.example: Vouching purchase invoice copies to gate entry registers and goods received notes to test purchase authenticity.
remember: Substantive procedures are mandatory for all material items regardless of control strength.
mistakes: Completely skipping substantive testing on material balances just because control risk is assessed as very low.

quiz.q: Substantive procedures must be performed for material classes of transactions:
o: Only when internal controls are completely absent
Irrespective of the assessed risks of material misstatement
quiz.why: SA 330 mandates substantive procedures for each material class of transaction, balance, and disclosure regardless of assessed risk.

quiz.q: Tests of details consist of which two parts?
o: Tests of transactions (vouching) and Tests of balances (verification)
quiz.why: Tests of details are categorized into vouching (transactions) and verification (account balances).

topics.title: Internal Financial Controls (IFC) - Regulatory Requirements
explain: Internal Financial Controls (IFC) cover financial reporting reliability, operational efficiency, asset safeguarding, and fraud prevention.
Sec 134(5)(e): Directors of listed companies must state that IFC is laid down, adequate, and operating effectively.
Sec 143(3)(i): Auditor's report must state whether company has adequate IFC system over financial reporting and its operating effectiveness.
Exemption from Sec 143(3)(i): One Person Companies (OPC), Small Companies, or Private Companies with Turnover < 50 Cr AND Aggregate Borrowings < 25 Cr.

flow.title: IFC Reporting Applicability for Private Companies
steps: If OPC or Small Company -> EXEMPT from Sec 143(3)(i)
If Private Co: Check Turnover (< 50 Cr) AND Borrowings (< 25 Cr)
If BOTH limits met -> EXEMPT from Auditor IFC Report
If limit exceeded -> Mandatory Auditor IFC Reporting

topics.example: A private company with Rs 40 Cr turnover and Rs 10 Cr bank loan is exempt from auditor IFC reporting under Sec 143(3)(i).
remember: IFC Auditor Exemption for Private Co: Turnover < 50 Cr AND Borrowings < 25 Cr.
mistakes: Thinking directors' IFC responsibility is limited only to financial reporting (for directors it covers operations/compliance too).

quiz.q: Under Section 134(5)(e) of the Companies Act, 2013, who has explicit responsibility to state that IFC is adequate and operating effectively?
quiz.why: Section 134(5)(e) casts this responsibility on directors of listed companies in their Directors' Responsibility Statement.

quiz.q: A private company is exempt from Auditor Reporting on IFC under Sec 143(3)(i) if its turnover is less than Rs 50 Crore AND borrowings are less than:
quiz.why: The statutory exemption threshold for private company borrowings from banks/FIs/bodies corporate is less than Rs 25 Crore.

topics.title: Automated Environment, IT Risks, Controls & Data Analytics
explain: An automated environment processes business transactions using IT systems (e.g., ERPs like SAP/Oracle).
IT Risks: Inaccurate data processing, unauthorized access, direct database changes (backend), lack of segregation of duties, data loss.
Controls: (A) General IT Controls (GITC - security, change mgmt, data centre), (B) Application Controls (input checks, limit checks), (C) IT-Dependent Controls.
Data Analytics / CAATs (using IDEA, ACL) allows auditors to test 100% data populations, check sample selection, and perform automated re-computations.

flow.title: Hierarchy of IT Controls and Data Analytics
steps: Apply CAATs / Data Analytics for 100% testing

topics.example: An ERP rule preventing entry of sales orders above user credit limit is an Application Control; server room access is a GITC.
remember: If General IT Controls (GITCs) fail, automated application controls cannot be relied upon.
mistakes: Treating IT-dependent manual controls as independent of IT reliability.

quiz.q: Controls operating directly at business process level embedded within software (like mandatory data entry fields) are called:
quiz.why: Application controls operate at the transaction/business process level within software applications.

quiz.q: What is the full form of CAATs used in data analytics for auditing?
quiz.why: CAATs stands for Computer Assisted Auditing Techniques.
